claims.text: The starting catalyst is a high-entropy automotive exhaust alloy containing near-equiatomic Ni, Co, Cu, Fe, and Al with trace Pt as its only platinum-group metal.
A rapid thermal redox treatment at approximately 750°C for about 10 minutes in 10 vol% H2O, 5 vol% H2, 0.1 vol% NO, and inert balance is the proposed intervention.
Immediate quenching in inert gas is part of the proposed treatment.
The specified treatment simulates transient engine operation.
Accurate redox control can restructure only the catalyst surface while leaving the bulk intact.
The redox treatment will form a nanoscale core–shell architecture.
The resulting shell will be an ultrathin Pt-enriched surface layer surrounding a high-entropy-alloy core.
Part of the reconstructed surface or interface will transition into a stabilized Al2O3 or mixed-oxide phase.
The high-temperature redox cycle promotes selective segregation of Pt and other catalytically active elements.
Selective segregation causes in-situ self-assembly of the nanostructured shell.
Steam induces controlled surface oxidation.
Controlled surface oxidation passivates the catalyst surface and limits sintering.
The reconstructed shell protects the catalyst against deactivation by H2O and NO.
The treatment preserves active Pt clusters under challenging exhaust conditions.
The treated catalyst will have significantly better low-temperature catalytic activity than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will resist H2O- and NO-induced deactivation better than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will have improved durability during transient operation and thermal aging.
The proposed treatment will maintain low overall platinum consumption.
Over-oxidation or treatment-induced sintering will negate the expected benefits.
The expected improvements are limited to accurately controlled treatment and simulated transient or accelerated high-mileage operating conditions.
